A story should leave your desk for another reader's hands only after you are satisfied that you have given it everything you have. It is natural to hand it first to the people you love most, and there is no harm in that. Yet in most cases their reading will not push the work forward in any meaningful way. The comments that truly improve a manuscript tend to come from elsewhere. Readers should be selected for the sharpness of their judgment, not for how dear they are to you. Other writers are the natural choice, though not every writer is equally useful. In a writing class or circle you soon learn whose pages you respect. You also learn, from experience, whose comments once helped you and whose merely flattered you.

In cultures that treat time flexibly, a meeting behaves less like a checklist and more like a growing plant. An agenda listing a start time and a topic is usually sent out beforehand. That document forms the central stem of the gathering. Nobody, however, assumes the conversation will march straight down the list. A concern that felt pressing when the agenda was written may matter far less today. So the talk turns aside, side conversations open up, and members step out for urgent calls. Managers there judge such detours as signs of health rather than failure. The best sessions, they believe, develop in directions nobody could have scheduled.

The phrase 'always on' describes a life of nonstop content intake. Alerts, likes, uploads, and replies arrive in an unbroken stream. When that stream overlaps with a meal, our capacity is overloaded. The will that digests virtual material cannot also attend to physical food. Skilled multi-taskers may seem to manage both, yet most people do not. They rush the sandwich and dash off a shortened, careless message. The message is misread, and the stomach protests soon afterward. Separating the two acts protects both the message and the meal.

A steady beat can settle a listener into ease, and that ease is pleasant on its own. Yet listeners almost always wait for something further to happen. Music therefore requires a process that builds strain and aims it at a destination. The thrill produced along that path is what turns listening into pleasure. Even a prelude without fixed measures follows the same rule. There the strain grows out of the rhythm's very vagueness. Its flowing motion prepares a release that arrives with the steady beat of the next movement. That release then seeds fresh strain, as surprising chords carry the piece onward.

Frederick Law Olmsted, remembered today as the father of American landscape architecture, was born in 1822. In his boyhood he frequently traveled through the countryside with his father, a man devoted to fine scenery. At fourteen he was getting ready to enroll at Yale College. A severe case of sumac poisoning ruined his eyesight, however, and he was never able to enter the school. Rather than going to college, he learned about the world by working as a clerk, a sailor, and a farmer. In 1858 he and Calvert Vaux won the competition to design New York City's Central Park with their "Greensward Plan." Throughout the Civil War he acted as General Secretary of the United States Sanitary Commission. After his death in 1903 his sons carried on his ideas, and in 1979 his Brookline home and office became a National Historic Site.

Capitalism is not a world saturated with money; it is a world in which small islands of cash exchange float on wide oceans of cheap nature. Sustaining human life inside those money relations costs a great deal, and the cost climbs steadily. Wages can be held down or even cut, yet the resulting inequality eventually produces crises and public unrest. Workers who demand dignity make their labor more expensive. Once a production process has burned through an island of resources, energy stops being cheap. As the climate shifts, harvests fall short of what they used to be. Every cheap thing the system depends on therefore becomes costly in time. This is why frontiers matter so much: they supply fresh places where cheap resources and cheap labor can still be taken.

③why climate change is the single cause of food shortages

⑤why island economies grow faster than continental ones

Buying a "green" product can make some shoppers feel entitled to cheat afterwards, because they count that purchase as a good deed. This moral licensing appears in environmental cooperation as well. Being reminded of one's own environmentally damaging actions leaves a residue of "eco-guilt." Those who feel it look for pro-environmental behaviors that will offset the guilt and bring their moral books back into balance. Because they want relief as fast and as effortlessly as possible, they are drawn to "quick-fixes." They may even revise how they judge their past damaging acts and their future green ones. The map of where humanity actually lives is losing its once-firm outlines. Because relocation has become an ordinary part of life, our species is undergoing something like a change of state. Matter melts from solid to liquid and then evaporates into gas as its molecules warm, drift apart and quicken. Human beings now behave in much the same way, resembling quantum particles whose speed and position never hold still. Many people would welcome a return to some older form of steadiness. Yet a quantum world simply does not offer that comfort to anyone who asks for it. The sheer complexity of modern life keeps making it harder to stay in one place for good. Wealthy remote workers, billionaires holding several passports and migrant laborers alike all belong to this expanding population.

Across psychology, theorists concur that mourning our losses matters, whether those losses are private or shared by a whole community. Grief is not a frozen feeling but a moving process that consciousness cannot do without. Psychologically, it lets us confront our own fragility and that of others, and it restores our energy after serious loss. Mourning pays respect to the sorrow and the sense of absence rather than pushing them aside. At the same time it prepares the soil in which personal change and continued life can take root. One psychotherapist calls this work an act of devotion grounded in love, one that demands continual attention and listening. Grieving what has gone opens a path toward deeper love for whatever still remains with us. In time that love becomes a wish to repair the damage done, or to make amends for it.

A digital twin is a virtual duplicate of an asset or an activity, built from models and sensor readings. The idea itself is hardly recent, since engineers have relied on 3D renderings and process simulations for many years. What has changed is the speed of wireless networks and the flood of real-time data they deliver. With that data, digital representations can be far more detailed and far more dynamic than before. Sensors on a connected device feed measurements back to the model without pause. The twin therefore mirrors the properties and states of the physical object as they actually are. Industries adopt such twins where equipment is expensive and stoppages are ruinous. Turbines, jet engines, and train engines are among the first machines to receive them.

Selecting surroundings that provide food, cover from predators, and access to mates shapes an animal's biological success. Research shows that animals do more than locate the richest patch available at the moment. They also judge how a place will serve requirements that have not yet arisen. The black-throated green warbler makes the point clearly. Early in summer it claims territory among red spruce, though those trees yield less food than nearby white spruce. Once nests hold hungry chicks, the red spruce turns out to offer the easier feeding. The bird has effectively chosen for a season it has not yet reached. Habitat choice is therefore a forecast as much as a preference.

A language is culture made audible. As children move through the stages of acquisition, they absorb more than vocabulary and grammar. What they take in are the interaction styles that make them effective speakers in each setting. In individualistic societies that style is direct, favoring categorical words such as absolutely or certainly. In collectivistic societies, values of interdependence and harmony pull speech toward maybe or perhaps. English alone among the world's languages capitalizes the pronoun for the self. Japanese, by contrast, offers no single equivalent of that pronoun. The word for the self shifts with situation, gender, age, and the listener's standing.

Density counts how many people occupy a space; crowding names the feeling that the space is too small. The two are usually linked, and high density often brings sensory overload and rising anxiety. Yet some psychologists refuse to treat crowding as automatically harmful. In their view it is a neutral force that magnifies whatever a person already feels. A fan eager for a concert therefore enjoys the show more because the hall is packed. Someone dreading the same evening finds the packed hall unbearable. Groups behave the same way, so an angry crowd grows angrier as it tightens. Parks and pedestrian streets, by lifting the prevailing mood, work in the opposite direction.

Behavioral economists use the term choice architecture for the way a decision setting shapes the decisions made inside it. In digital life, that setting is built almost entirely by algorithms. They decide which posts appear, which products are suggested, and which options are visible at all. Through that quiet editing, they push users toward certain routes rather than others. Sometimes the push is helpful, steering people toward healthier habits. But when the designers' aims differ from the user's welfare, the same push becomes manipulation. Guarding one's own judgment therefore takes deliberate work: seeking out unfamiliar viewpoints and refusing the obvious recommendation. It also takes remembering that an algorithm's data records what has already happened, not what ought to happen next.

Do not show your story to anyone until you are content that you have done everything you could for it. Showing it to family and close friends is perfectly fine as a pleasure, but it is a poor way to improve the work. Affection makes honest criticism difficult, and praise from loved ones rarely reveals what is broken. The most useful responses usually come from readers with no stake in your feelings. Therefore, pick your readers for the sharpness of their critical eye rather than for their nearness to you. Other writers make good candidates, but do not assume that any writer will serve. Within a class or a writing group you will discover whose work you genuinely admire. Past experience will also tell you whose comments truly helped and whose did not.

We like to believe that answering messages during lunch saves us time. In truth our will can digest only one kind of content at a time. While it works on virtual material, its forces are pulled away from the meal. The text that results is half-hearted and shortened into near-nonsense. The recipient misreads it, and further messages are needed to repair the damage. Meanwhile the food goes down unnoticed and settles as nervous indigestion. Nothing is truly gained by pressing the two activities into the same minutes. Finish the sandwich, taste it, let it settle, and only then reach for the phone.

A meeting in a flexible-time culture like those found in South America, parts of Europe, Africa, and the Middle East is more like an evergreen tree. An agenda with a meeting start time and a topic will probably be circulated before the meeting. This will serve as the trunk of the tree. But there's no expectation that the meeting will progress in a linear manner. What seemed like a priority last week when the agenda was crafted is not necessarily the priority right now ― so discussion may branch off in a new direction. Other branches may sprout as some members have urgent phone calls that take them in and out of the meeting. Or sub-groups may form within the room to discuss timely subjects linked in some way to the main meeting trunk. In flexible-time cultures, it seems clear that the most productive meetings grow in unpredictable ways, and the effective manager is flexible and professional enough to capitalize on priorities and changing needs as they arise. Interruptions, agenda changes, and frequent shifts in direction are seen as natural and necessary.

Progressive educators and librarians are developing curricula to teach what we might call attention literacy. This means helping students recognize, for example, how the architecture of a social media feed or a news site is deliberately designed to distract or provoke them. Classes in media literacy traditionally cover how to evaluate the credibility of sources ― now they also include recognizing clickbait, understanding the role of algorithms in what content is served up, and observing one's own patterns of distraction. A student might be tasked with tracking how many times they switch tasks or check their phone in an hour of homework, to raise self-awareness about fragmentation. Capitalism is not a system where cash is everywhere but rather one in which islands of cash exchange exist within oceans of cheap―or potentially cheap―natures. Reproducing life within the cash nexus is expensive, and it grows more expensive over time. Workers' wages can be frozen, even rolled back, but in the end inequality leads to crises of the kind we've recently seen bring about populist protests in the United States and the United Kingdom. Workers demand dignity, and their labor becomes expensive. Production processes burn through an island, and energy is no longer cheap. The climate changes, and crops can no longer grow as abundantly as they once did. Frontiers are so important in these processes because they offer places where the new cheap things can be seized ―and the cheap work of humans and other natures can be forcefully taken.

When people are reminded of deeds they have done that they know were harmful to the environment, they might be left with a feeling of "eco-guilt." People who experience eco-guilt seek pro-environmental actions to compensate for this guilt and restore balance. Of the cognitive motivations, the most fundamental one encourages people to understand their environment to predict what is going to happen in case of uncertainties. Most important, people prefer to develop meanings that are shared with other people. For example, if in a given year more people accept offers of admission than a college expects, quite a few students end up living in dorm lounges or campus hotels. It is easy to understand why living in the lounge is problematic (no closet, for one thing). But what is wrong with a room at campus hotels? After all, students in a hotel get private bathrooms, their own TV, and larger rooms. In fact, living in those hotels is problematic because the student residents are not a part of a stable group with people who will be their neighbors for the year; they must wait in uncertainty before finding their social niche. The uncertainty itself is the problem. People lack a shared social understanding, normally developed from membership in a stable group.

Psychological theories across the field agree on the importance of grieving our losses, from the highly personal through to the broadly collective. Grief is a dynamic emotional process essential to consciousness. At a psychological level, it supports us to both face into our own and others' vulnerability, transience and mortality, and to repair life energy after significant loss. Grief work honours the loss, the sadness and the experience of diminishment or absence, while also setting up the ground for self-transformation and the continuation of life. Psychotherapist Fran Weller describes grief work is "an act of devotion, rooted in love and compassion" that requires "an ongoing practice of deepening, attending and listening." When we grieve for what is lost, it clears the way towards a strengthening of love and commitment for what remains. In time this may build a desire to make good from the loss by repairing as many damages as we can and/or compensating for them. Grief can make us both very sad and very motivated to act.
Grief work the loss, the sadness and the experience of diminishment or absence.

When we focus on the obvious aspects of media, we miss the changes that accumulate over time but are not apparent day to day. Most of us notice the obvious aspects of a new medium or technology while missing the more subtle aspects. Take, for example, the microwave oven. It was introduced in the early 1980s and revolutionized food preparation. Traditionally, one person spent the better part of an afternoon fixing an evening meal for a family. Now, it was possible to prepare foods very quickly, and this shortening of preparation time was liberating for the cooks in the family, most of whom tended to be women. But the short-term, obvious implications of greater convenience made it easy to overlook the long-term implications of no longer having one person fix food for the family to eat together at an evening meal. As time went on, fewer and fewer families sat down together to eat dinner. Meals that took a long time to prepare became a luxury of the past, except perhaps for special occasions. The effects of the microwave oven on family life were not anticipated and would have been difficult to foresee.
We miss the changes that over time but are not apparent day to day.

Digital twins are digital replicas of assets or activities using modeling and sensors to create digital representations. Digital twins are not new; engineering teams in various industries have used 3D renderings of computer-aided design models, asset models, and process simulations for years. However, faster wireless networks and the resulting availability of real-time data enable much more detailed and dynamic digital representations. When sensors collect data from a connected device, the sensor data can be used to continuously update the digital twin. The digital twin becomes a real-time accurate copy of a physical object's properties and states. Similarly, the twin fails to capture emotional or cultural factors, limiting discussions beyond strictly technical contexts. For instance, digital twins of physical assets such as power-generation turbines, jet engines, and train engines are becoming common when the assets are very valuable and when downtime would be very costly.

The ability to select a set of surroundings suitable for foraging, shelter from predators, and the availability of mates is one of the most important determinants of biological success ― measured as survival to reproductive age and the production of offspring. Many studies have shown that not only do animals have a remarkable ability to seek out the best available locations for the necessities of life, but that they are able to anticipate how a setting will serve their future needs. For example, the black-throated green warbler, a small songbird that nests in spruce forests of eastern North America, establishes territories preferentially among the red spruce trees early in the summer months, even though these trees offer less food than the neighboring white spruce trees. Later, though, when nests are built and hungry baby birds need nourishment, it is the red spruce forest that offers the easier pickings. Somehow, the warbler has been guided to settle in locations that will suit its future parenting needs better than its present ones.
Animals can not only find good locations but also how a setting will serve their future needs.

Language is a manifestation of culture. At different language acquisition stages, children do not learn language per se; rather they learn the various patterns and styles of language interaction that enable them to function as competent communicators in different situational contexts. They develop a culture-specific communication style that is, for example, direct and explicit in individualistic cultures or indirect and implicit in collectivistic cultures. Examples of words linked with the direct style are categorical words like absolutely, certainly, or positively. By contrast, the cultural assumptions of interdependence and harmony require that collectivists limit themselves to implicit and even ambiguous use of words, using terms like maybe, perhaps, or probably. The English language is the only language in the world that spells I with a capital letter. This phenomenon may reflect the fact that the roots of individualism are in England. Environmental psychologists make a distinction between the physical measurement of density (how many people are in a particular space) and crowding (the psychological feeling of not having enough space). Usually, high density is needed for the phenomenon of crowding, which makes people experience sensory overload, a lack of control, and rising stress and anxiety. However, some psychologists see crowding as neutral rather than invariably negative, and believe that people's moods and behaviors intensify as density increases. So if an individual is looking forward to a concert, say, the feeling of crowding enhances their enjoyment of the performance. But if they are dreading an event, crowding will make the person's experience of it even worse. Put into a community setting, crowding may accentuate the dominant behavior ― an aggressive group may turn violent as density rises. Conversely, creating positive social spaces such as parks and pedestrian areas in high-density urban environments may help to lift the general mood and defuse tension.
Building parks and pedestrian areas in dense cities may lift the general mood and tension.

Our adult brains retain a preference for perpetuating good, fair behavior. Simply perceiving ourselves as people who do good deeds and behaving accordingly motivates us to do greater good in the future. In one paid study of one hundred college students, subjects who wrote down a list of past good deeds and were then asked to donate money to a charity gave, on average, over half the earnings they'd made from the study — almost twice as much as those who had been instructed to recall previous bad deeds. In addition, subjects who'd taken pains to describe not only how they'd been nice to others but how people responded were likely to donate significantly less than those who focused purely on the actions themselves. In other words, people who seemed concerned about appearances (e.g., the impact of their good deed, as much as the deed itself) were less generous than those who cared more about doing good for its own sake.

The concept of "choice architecture," popularized in behavioral economics, highlights how the design of the environment in which choices are made can significantly influence the decisions people make. Algorithms are, in essence, sophisticated architects of our digital environments. By curating what we see, what we are recommended, and what options are presented to us, they subtly, and sometimes not so subtly, nudge us towards particular paths. While nudges can be used for beneficial purposes, such as encouraging healthier habits, they also carry the potential for manipulation, particularly when the underlying objectives of the architects are not aligned with the well-being or autonomy of the individual. The question then becomes: how can we cultivate and protect our human agency in an increasingly algorithmic world? It requires a conscious effort to maintain critical engagement with the technologies we use. It means actively seeking out diverse perspectives, following algorithmic recommendations, and making deliberate choices that go against the predicted grain. It involves cultivating a healthy skepticism towards the seemingly objective outputs of algorithms and remembering that these systems are designed by humans with specific goals, and that their data is a reflection of past realities, not necessarily a prescription for future flourishing.
Their data is a reflection of past realities, not necessarily a for future flourishing.

Ridge was a high school student who wanted to major in music in college. For weeks, on his balcony, every night he listened to a man playing the guitar in the apartment across the courtyard. Although the songs the man played were all new to Ridge, he somehow managed to attach his own made-up lyrics to them. One night, Ridge slid open the balcony door and stepped outside. He told his mom he was going out to the balcony to do his homework. The man was playing the guitar on his balcony as usual and Ridge started to mindlessly follow the rhythm. While Ridge was singing along to the music, the man suddenly stopped playing. He had never stopped in the middle of a song, so naturally Ridge looked in his direction. The man held up his index finger as if to say, "Hold on." He lifted one sheet of paper, and Ridge narrowed his eyes to get a good look at what was written on it. His phone number and "Text me" were written on the sheet. Then he flipped the paper over and wrote, "I have a question." Curious about the man's question, and wondering why he had asked for a text instead of a call, Ridge pulled out his phone and entered the number. He typed, "What's your question?" The man texted, "I want to know how you're singing lyrics to my songs when I haven't even added lyrics to them yet." Ridge was greatly surprised. Why hadn't he thought the man could see him sitting out there? He had never thought the man had noticed him singing along to his music. The man sent another message asking, "Will you send them to me?" After reading the man's message asking for his lyrics, Ridge hesitated. Ridge loved writing lyrics, but he had never shared anything he'd written with anyone. Eventually, he wrote down one of his favorite lyrics and sent it to him. A few days later, a new message came from the man. He wanted to use Ridge's lyrics for his new album. It turned out he was a deaf guitarist and songwriter in a band called Brennan's Band.
It turned out he was a guitarist and songwriter in a band called Brennan's Band.
